title: Katherine M. Kennedy
text:
Katherine M. Kennedy

  ORCID·Google Scholar·LinkedIn·GitHub





Each pregnancy reshapes the gut microbial community that the next child inherits. I study how a mother’s pregnancy history and diet shape the gut and microbiota her child starts life with, and how those early differences carry forward across the lifespan. I am a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biochemistry and Biomedical Sciences at McMaster University.

My work on low-biomass methods established that meconium has no detectable microbiota before birth, so colonization begins at birth and what the mother transmits during delivery matters. I have since shown that the maternal gut microbiome adapts differently to a first pregnancy than to later ones, and that birth order changes how the neonatal microbiome responds to delivery mode and intrapartum antibiotics. In mice, maternal high-fat diet alters the fetal gut, with effects on the offspring microbiome and gut barrier that last into adulthood.
I work at the bench and the keyboard, from culturing and banking bacterial strains to shotgun metagenomics and TALDA, a method I developed with McMaster’s Department of Mathematics and Statistics to model microbial subcommunities over time. I designed and lead the Good Bugs Study, which tracks which vaginal and gut strains pass from mothers to newborns in first and later pregnancies. The Research page has the details.
Outside the lab, I spent five years as a sailing instructor. These days I make pottery and stained glass and am learning to knit. Charlie, my St. Bernard, supervises.

title: Katherine M. Kennedy
text:
Research
First and later pregnancies differ biologically, yet most studies of the maternal and infant microbiome treat them as interchangeable. My research asks how a mother’s pregnancy history and diet shape the gut and microbiota her child starts life with, and which of those early differences last into childhood and later life. The work combines human birth cohorts, mouse models of developmental programming, and methods built for low-biomass and longitudinal microbiome data.



The maternal gut microbiome adapts differently to a first pregnancy than to later ones, and birth order shapes neonatal colonization from the first days of life.

First-born children are smaller at birth, one sign that first and later pregnancies differ biologically. In a prospective cohort at Charité–Universitätsmedizin Berlin, I found that parity modifies how BMI and gestational weight gain relate to the maternal gut microbiota. Associations between excess adiposity and community composition were largely confined to first pregnancies, and multiparous participants followed different microbial trajectories. In a second pregnancy cohort (Bugs in BHIP), subcommunities of co-occurring taxa expanded and contracted differently in first and later pregnancies, and their postpartum recovery diverged. Pooling primiparous and multiparous participants can therefore obscure real biological signal.
The differences extend to the newborn. In neonates, delivery mode, birth order, and sex each independently shape early colonization, and birth order modifies how delivery mode and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) affect colonization in the first days of life. In the Baby & Mi birth cohort (245 infants, sampled from 3 days to 3 years), I am asking whether these differences persist through early childhood and whether they track with growth and atopic outcomes.

Papers: Kennedy et al. 2023, Gut Microbes · Kennedy et al. 2025, Gut Microbes · Kennedy et al. 2026, Gut Microbes




Birth-order differences in the infant microbiome are present within the first day of life. Because the fetal gut has no detectable microbiota before birth, these differences likely arise from what the mother transmits during delivery. I designed and lead the Good Bugs Study, funded by a Farncombe Innovation Grant, which uses culture-informed metagenomics to track which maternal vaginal and gut strains colonize newborns in first and later pregnancies. The study banks isolates for functional testing, including strains that may limit mother-to-infant transmission of potential pathogens.




In mice, maternal high-fat diet disrupts the gut–placenta–fetus axis, and its effects on the offspring gut persist into adulthood.

My doctoral work used a mouse model of diet-induced obesity to trace how maternal diet affects the gut–placenta–fetus axis. Characterizing the maternal gut microbiome, maternal intestine, placenta, and fetal intestine in the same cohort revealed a chain running from diet to fetus: disrupted maternal intestinal adaptation to pregnancy, placental hypoxia, and altered barrier protein and immune marker profiles in the fetal gut. That chain is not visible in studies of a single compartment.
Follow-up work showed that the fetal intestinal inflammation depends on TNF signalling, and that the effects persist. In adulthood, offspring had altered gut microbiota composition, increased gut barrier permeability, and greater susceptibility to a postnatal dietary challenge.

Papers: Gohir, Kennedy et al. 2019, J Physiol · PhD thesis, McMaster University, 2021





Meconium collected before birth has no detectable microbiota, so gut colonization begins at birth.

Reports of bacterial DNA in placenta, amniotic fluid, and meconium suggested that colonization begins in utero. Most of those studies lacked the contamination controls that low-biomass samples require. When a sample contains very little microbial DNA, reagent- and laboratory-derived sequences can dominate the result while still looking biologically plausible. Through a collaboration with Charité, I applied contamination-aware protocols to meconium collected immediately before caesarean delivery and found no detectable microbiota. I then re-analysed the published data behind a high-profile paper that I thought overstated the evidence for fetal microbial exposure, which became a peer-reviewed letter in Cell, and led a Nature perspective with 47 colleagues setting out principles for contamination-aware study design. That attention to technical artefacts goes back to my MSc work, which showed that PCR amplification introduces consistent, primer- and region-dependent biases in Illumina-based 16S rRNA gene profiling.
Longitudinal microbiome studies usually track individual taxa or diversity metrics over time. With McMaster’s Department of Mathematics and Statistics, I developed TALDA, which adapts latent Dirichlet allocation to model subcommunities of co-occurring taxa over time. In the Bugs in BHIP cohort it detected parity-dependent dynamics that conventional methods missed, and the approach applies to longitudinal microbiome data well beyond pregnancy.

Papers: Kennedy et al. 2021, Nat Microbiol · Kennedy et al. 2021, Cell · Kennedy et al. 2023, Nature · Kennedy et al. 2014, Appl Environ Microbiol · Kennedy et al. 2026, Gut Microbes




The question that runs through all of this work is which early-life differences last, and which can be changed. The next step is to follow them forward, from childhood growth and allergy to gut barrier function and health in aging, and to ask where along that path prevention could start.
Early-life programming is well established as a factor in who is susceptible to diet- and lifestyle-related disease. Whether it also shapes who benefits from interventions, such as changes in diet or exercise, is largely untested, and the answer could help match prevention to the people most likely to benefit.
